a: Throughout history, women have made profound contributions to mathematics despite often facing significant barriers to education and recognition. Hypatia of Alexandria (c. 360-415 CE) was one of the earliest known female mathematicians, known for her work in geometry and astronomy. She was the head of the Neoplatonic school in Alexandria. Sophie Germain (1776-1831) made groundbreaking contributions to number theory and elasticity theory, corresponding with Carl Friedrich Gauss under a male pseudonym. She developed what is now known as Germain's theorem for Fermat's Last Theorem. Ada Lovelace (1815-1852) is considered the world's first computer programmer for her work on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, creating the first algorithm intended for machine processing. Sofia Kovalevskaya (1850-1891) was the first woman to earn a doctorate in mathematics (from the University of Göttingen) and made important contributions to partial differential equations and mechanics. Emmy Noether (1882-1935) revolutionized abstract algebra and theoretical physics with Noether's theorem, which establishes the fundamental connection between symmetries and conservation laws. She is considered one of the most important mathematicians of the 20th century. Katherine Johnson (1918-2020) was a NASA mathematician whose calculations of orbital mechanics were critical to the success of early spaceflights, including John Glenn's orbit and the Apollo moon landing. Maryam Mirzakhani (1977-2017) was the first woman to win the Fields Medal (the highest honor in mathematics) for her work on the dynamics and geometry of Riemann surfaces.
